title: WHY DID GOD KILL SO MANY PEOPLE IN THE OLD TESTAMENT?
paragraphs: WHY DID GOD KILL SO MANY PEOPLE IN THE OLD TESTAMENT?
The Question Christians Are Afraid to Ask—and the Answer That Leads Through Judgment, Blood, Mercy, and a Cross Where God Himself Took the Sentence
There is a question sitting quietly in the back of many Christians’ minds.
Some are terrified to say it out loud.
Some unbelievers have already said it for them.
Some walked away from Christianity because nobody gave them an answer deeper than, “God can do whatever He wants.”
And some still sit in church, sing the songs, raise their hands, read their Bible...
then reach passages where entire populations die and quietly wonder:

How can the God who tells us not to murder be the same God who brought the Flood, destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, struck Egypt with plagues, judged Israel repeatedly, and commanded warfare against the Canaanites?
Why did God kill so many people in the Old Testament?
Scripture doesn't need us to protect it from difficult questions.
And God does not become more glorious when Christians pretend troubling passages aren't there.
But there is something you need to know before we go any further.
If you stay with this question long enough, something uncomfortable happens.
Eventually, the question stops being about them.
Because the most disturbing truth in these Old Testament judgments may not be that God judged sinners.
It may be that we have quietly begun believing that sinners are entitled to life from a holy God.
The Bible begins not with death, but life.
“In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth” (Genesis 1:1).
Humanity did not create itself. Life was not something Adam wrestled from God's possession. Breath was given.
Genesis says God formed man from the dust and breathed into him the breath of life.
Life, from the first page of Scripture, is gift.
God tells Adam concerning the forbidden tree:
The Hebrew construction intensifies the certainty of death.
God did not hide the consequence.

That matters because one of our greatest mistakes when reading the Old Testament is beginning with the assumption that human beings are morally innocent and God suddenly interrupts history with inexplicable violence.
That is not the biblical story.

The biblical story is that humanity received life from God, rebelled against the Giver of life, and unleashed sin, corruption, oppression, bloodshed, idolatry, exploitation, and death into His creation.
By Genesis 6, humanity's corruption had become horrifying.
Scripture describes human wickedness as great and the inclination of the human heart as continually evil.
Then comes a detail people sometimes forget when talking about the Flood.
God is not portrayed as enjoying what humanity had become.
Genesis 6:6 says His heart was grieved.
The Judge is grieved by the world He judges.
Biblical judgment is not presented as divine sadism.
God does not look at suffering the way a cruel spectator looks at entertainment.
Later, through Ezekiel, God explicitly declares:
The sense is, “Do I take any pleasure in the death of the wicked?” (Ezekiel 18:23).
The verse continues by contrasting death with God's desire that the wicked turn from his way and live.
That same heartbeat appears again in Ezekiel 33:11: God says He has no pleasure in the death of the wicked, but desires that the wicked turn and live.
God does not delight in evil's destruction.
Both truths belong in our theology.
Remove judgment, and holiness becomes sentimental.
Remove compassion, and holiness becomes monstrous.
This is where the question becomes especially difficult.
Israel enters the land. Battles happen. Cities fall. The Hebrew Bible sometimes uses the language of חֵרֶם — ḥērem, a term associated with something devoted to destruction or placed under the ban.
These passages should disturb casual readers.
We should never read them with a grin, and we should never turn them into permission for religious violence today.
Ancient Israel's conquest was a unique event within Israel's covenant history, not a standing authorization for Christians to kill God's enemies.
Jesus did not commission His church to conquer nations with swords.
He commanded disciples to make disciples of the nations.
The kingdom advances through Gospel proclamation, sacrificial love, witness, suffering, and the power of the Holy Spirit—not through Christians slaughtering unbelievers.
But why was Canaan judged at all?
Here is a detail that changes the conversation.
God did not simply find a random group of innocent people, give their land to His favorites, and order their extermination.
Centuries earlier, God told Abraham that his descendants would not yet possess the land because:
“the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full” (Genesis 15:16).
The same Old Testament that records divine judgment also records extraordinary divine patience.
If the conquest narrative were merely racial favoritism, Israel should have enjoyed immunity.
God warned Israel that if they practiced the same abominations, the land would “vomit” them out too (Leviticus 18).
Eventually Israel descended into idolatry, injustice, oppression, sexual immorality, violence, and even child sacrifice.
The people were carried into exile.
Being chosen does not make evil holy.
Israel's covenant status did not turn sin into righteousness.
The Judge of the nations also judged His covenant people.
And suddenly another assumption begins collapsing.
Maybe the Bible's scandal is not that God takes sin too seriously.
Maybe our scandal is that we don't take it seriously enough.
We live in an age where we want God to stop evil...
but become offended when He judges evildoers.
We ask why God didn't stop the murderer.
Why didn't He stop the abuser?
Why didn't He stop the trafficker?
Why didn't He stop the tyrant?
But when Scripture shows God intervening decisively against evil, we ask:
We want a God who stops evil...
as long as He never judges sinners.
At the secret things we hope nobody ever discovers?
If God removed every source of evil from the world tonight...
would you and I still be here tomorrow morning?
That is where this question becomes personal.
We naturally divide humanity into “bad people” and people like us.
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God” (Romans 3:23).

The Hebrew prophets understood sin as more than occasional mistakes. Sin is rebellion against the holy Creator. It corrupts relationships, societies, worship, justice, sexuality, power, families, nations, and ultimately the human heart.
And the New Testament does not soften this.
τὰ γὰρ ὀψώνια τῆς ἁμαρτίας θάνατος
ta gar opsōnia tēs hamartias thanatos
“For the wages of sin is death...” (Romans 6:23).
That word ὀψώνια — opsōnia refers to wages, pay, what is received as compensation.
Thank God he doesn't stop there.
Because the verse turns on one of the most beautiful contrasts in Scripture:
τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος
to de charisma tou Theou zōē aiōnios
“but the gift of God is eternal life...”
ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ Κυρίῳ ἡμῶν
Now we are standing at the center of Christianity.
Christianity's answer is not that God simply pretends evil never happened.
The cross tells us something terrifying about sin.
Forgiveness is free to the sinner, but it was not cheap.
There was a crown of thorns.
And hanging there was not another Canaanite.
The One who had no sin.
This is where the entire question begins turning inside out.
At the cross, God did not remain distant from the judgment human rebellion deserves.
In Christian theology, God the Son took flesh and willingly gave Himself for sinners.
“He was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities” (Isaiah 53:5).
Paul later writes that God made Christ, who knew no sin, to be sin for us so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God (2 Corinthians 5:21).
Peter says Christ “bare our sins in his own body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24).
The Gospel does not answer the Old Testament's judgment by saying:
Jesus stepped beneath judgment to save His enemies.
Not God pretending sin doesn't matter.
God dealing with sin at unimaginable cost.
The cross is where divine justice and divine mercy meet without either being erased.
And this is why Jesus Himself refuses to let discussions about tragic death remain academic.
When people told Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate, Jesus rejected the assumption that their deaths proved they were worse sinners than everyone else.
Then He spoke words modern ears find uncomfortable:
“unless ye repent, ye shall all likewise perish.”
He made the same point concerning eighteen people killed when a tower fell in Siloam. Their deaths did not mean they were uniquely guilty. Jesus turned the question toward the living:
The Greek word is connected with μετανοέω — metanoeō, to repent, to turn, to undergo a fundamental change of mind and direction.
Jesus takes our obsession with asking why those people died...
and turns our eyes toward the condition of our own souls.
That may be the moment this article becomes uncomfortable.
Because maybe you clicked this expecting an argument about dead people thousands of years ago.
And perhaps the greater mystery isn't:
“Why did God judge so many people?”
Perhaps another question deserves to haunt us:
Why has God shown so much patience toward me?
The pornography you keep deleting from your history but not from your life.
The person you refuse to forgive.
The money that became your god.
The church face covering the private addiction.
The Bible verses posted publicly while your private world is collapsing.
The nights when you knew exactly what God was telling you to leave...
That breath is not proof that sin doesn't matter.
It is an opportunity for repentance.
Do not mistake God's patience for God's approval.
But do not mistake His holiness for unwillingness to forgive either.
The Bible gives us astonishing examples.
Rahab lived in Jericho, a city destined for judgment.
And then grace did something scandalous.
The woman associated with Jericho became woven into Israel's story.
Matthew even names Rahab in the genealogy leading to Jesus Christ.
A woman living under the shadow of judgment becomes part of the family line through which Scripture traces the Messiah.
That is judgment not getting the final sentence over the person who turns toward God.
Yet when Nineveh repented, God relented from the announced destruction.
Jonah became angry precisely because he knew what kind of God he was dealing with.
He complained that God was gracious, compassionate, slow to anger, and abundant in steadfast love.
Imagine being angry because God forgave your enemies.
Then ask whether there is a little Jonah hiding inside us.
Justice for everyone who hurt us.
The Old Testament is not one long story of an angry God killing people until gentle Jesus arrives to calm Him down.
That caricature cannot survive careful reading.
Judgment appears in the New Testament.
The same Jesus who welcomed sinners also warned repeatedly about judgment.
The same Old Testament God who judged nations repeatedly showed mercy, patience, covenant love, and forgiveness.
The holy and loving God judges evil, pursues sinners, provides atonement, calls people to repentance, and ultimately reveals His saving purpose in Jesus Christ.
God does not save sinners by declaring evil good.
The grave does not get the last word.
Judgment does not get the final sentence over those who are in Christ.
That is why Romans 6:23 begins like a funeral and ends like resurrection:
You can almost hear the dirt hitting the coffin.
“...the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
Jesus walked out of a tomb.
So no, we should not sanitize the Old Testament.
We should not pretend its judgments are easy.
We should not mock people who struggle with these passages.
We should not use shallow answers where careful biblical thinking is required.
And Christians should certainly never use Israel's ancient wars as justification for hatred, cruelty, ethnic superiority, or violence.
But neither should we put God in the defendant's chair while quietly assuming humanity is innocent.
The biblical claim is much more confronting.
Maybe you have spent years angry with God.
Maybe someone used religion to wound you.
Maybe Christians gave you clichés when your questions deserved compassion and serious answers.
Maybe you have been pretending faith while secretly drifting farther from Christ.
Maybe nobody around you knows how tired your soul has become.
And the invitation of the Gospel is not “clean yourself up enough so God can tolerate you.”
Bring the parts of your story you wish you could burn.
Jesus Christ did not come for people who had successfully rewritten themselves.
If this exposed something you've been hiding, don't manufacture a religious response.
And believers reading those words—don't turn somebody else's vulnerability into gossip.
Maybe they would never enter a church.
Maybe they stopped believing Christians were willing to wrestle with hard questions.
Because one day the question may return, and when it does, you need to remember where Scripture ultimately takes us:
and then to an empty tomb.
And if Gospel Warrior has helped you understand Scripture, return to Christ, or confront questions you were afraid to ask, stay close to this ministry.
Supporting Gospel work is not what saves you, earns God's favor, proves that you love Him, or purchases spiritual blessing. Jesus alone saves, and grace cannot be bought.
But one way believers may freely glorify God is by generously supporting and sharing faithful Gospel ministry so biblical truth can keep reaching people who desperately need Christ.
You cannot purchase the grace of God.
And the greatest way to respond is to belong completely to Christ.
Support Gospel work freely if God leads you.
Because after all the difficult passages, all the uncomfortable questions, all the judgments, all the graves, all the rebellion, all the blood, and all the human failure...
The Bible's greatest scandal is not that sinners were judged; it is that the Judge stepped into our story, bore the cost of saving sinners, and opened the way home.
